q: Which policy deals with safe ways to raise concerns, with protection from retaliation?
o: Whistleblowing, with clear protection from retaliation for reporters
Anti-harassment, with clear rules on workplace bullying behaviour
Data protection, with rules on storing case records
Modern slavery, with steps on supply chain risks
why: The whistleblowing policy protects people who raise concerns in good faith.

q: When should a safeguarding policy be reviewed?
o: At least every two years or after any incident
Only when a donor requests a fresh signed version
Every ten years alongside the long strategic plan cycle
Never, because a signed policy stays valid for ever
why: Policies should be reviewed at least every two years or after an incident.

q: What should the scope of a safeguarding policy cover?
o: Staff, volunteers, consultants, partners, visitors and every programme setting
Permanent staff only, in the head office and sites
Staff and volunteers only, during working hours at sites
Children only, in classroom settings run by the organisation
why: The scope must include everyone linked to the organisation, in every setting.

q: What should confidentiality provisions in a policy state?
o: What is private, what is shared, with whom, including legal exceptions
That all details are shared with every staff member for transparency
That nothing is ever shared with anyone, including the police authorities
That information is shared only when a donor requests a copy
why: Confidentiality means sharing only what is needed with those who need it, with legal exceptions.

q: Who should sign the statement of commitment in a policy, and why?
o: Leadership, showing that safeguarding is a clear organisational priority
The SFP/DSL alone, showing that safeguarding is specialist work
The newest staff member, showing that everyone shares responsibility
The donor's representative, showing that funders approve every policy
why: Leadership signs to show safeguarding is a priority.

q: Which feature must a reporting procedure include?
o: An anonymous option, plus who reports to whom, when
A single named channel, with strict office hours only
A verbal route only, with no written records kept
A donor route only, with no internal staff channel
why: A reporting procedure needs clear steps, timelines and an anonymous option.

q: A policy says staff are trained within 30 days. What does a procedure add?
o: Who acts, when, how, where it is recorded and who checks
A longer promise, a bolder tone and a signed leadership letter
A donor logo, a printed cover and a numbered page layout
A legal opinion, a court filing and a sworn notarised copy
why: A procedure adds who, when, how, where recorded and who checks.

q: In the 30-day training example, who confirms there is no unsupervised contact until training is done?
o: The line manager, using a supervision plan from day one
The new volunteer, using a self-declaration form on day one
The donor, using a monitoring checklist from the first month
The board, using an annual audit from the first year
why: The line manager confirms this using a supervision plan from day one.

q: Which consultation practice is correct with children?
o: Ask in age-suitable ways and never ask for abuse details in groups
Ask in group sessions and require each child to describe any harm
Ask only caregivers and then summarise the children's views on their behalf
Ask once a year and then never report back on what changed
why: Ask children in age-suitable ways and never ask them to describe abuse in a group.

q: What should happen to findings from safeguarding consultations?
o: Feed into risk assessments and plans, with feedback to communities
Stay in the report folder until the next donor visit
Be summarised for the board but hidden from the communities
Be used only to design the next donor fundraising campaign
why: Findings must go back into risk assessments and plans, and communities should hear what changed.

q: Which is a sign of an unhealthy safeguarding culture?
o: Concerns are handled quietly to protect organisational reputation
Reporters are thanked, protected and told what changed
Safeguarding sits on routine meeting agendas every month
Mistakes lead to open learning rather than blame
why: Handling concerns quietly to protect reputation is a sign of an unhealthy culture.

q: Which is the first of the five ways to shift safeguarding culture?
o: Leaders go first by visibly championing and following the standards
Staff go first by reporting every colleague's small mistake publicly
Donors go first by writing much stricter conditions into contracts
Communities go first by reporting before any training ever happens
why: Leaders must go first and follow the same standards.

q: A senior staff member breaks the code and a leader says he has served for years. What does a healthy culture require?
o: Hold everyone to the same standard, including long-serving senior staff
Allow a quiet warning because seniority earns some extra tolerance
Delay action until the donor has finished its current review
Move him to another site so the problem leaves quietly
why: Leaders must hold everyone to the standard, including senior staff.

q: Why does a strong culture outlast individual people?
o: Shared values survive staff turnover, but one lead does not
Written policies survive staff turnover, but shared values do not
Signed forms survive staff turnover, but daily habits do not
Donor funding survives staff turnover, but local trust does not
why: A single safeguarding person leaves, but shared values and habits remain.

q: Which duty belongs to the board or trustees?
o: Oversee governance, carry legal responsibility and review safeguarding reports
Receive every concern first and record it in registers
Deliver all induction training and brief every visiting vendor
Collect reference checks and keep every personnel file safe
why: The board oversees governance, carries legal responsibility and reviews reports.

q: Which action is NOT part of the SFP/DSL role?
o: Investigate serious allegations alone to save the organisation precious time
Record each report in the confidential register the same day
Escalate concerns to leaders and refer survivors to support services
Lead induction training and brief partners, vendors and visiting guests
why: The SFP/DSL never investigates alone.

q: What gives an SFP/DSL real authority?
o: Right to escalate, pause unsafe activities and reach the board
A title on the door and a mention in handbooks
A donor letter and a place on the finance committee
Personal friendship with the director and a flexible office timetable
why: Authority means the right to escalate, pause unsafe activities and reach the board.

q: Which job description clause is best for a Programme Officer?
o: Complete a risk assessment before every activity involving children or adults at risk
Support the safeguarding team whenever time allows during the normal busy working week
Be aware of safeguarding issues and try to avoid any very serious mistakes
Attend safeguarding training when invited and share the slides with your close colleagues
why: A good clause is specific, measurable and tied to the work.

q: What should the yearly performance plan include?
o: One safeguarding objective for each person, discussed in reviews
One safeguarding objective for the SFP/DSL, discussed once yearly
No safeguarding objective because it belongs in the policy
A safeguarding objective only for staff meeting young children
why: Every yearly plan should carry one safeguarding objective, reviewed with the line manager.

q: Which set describes a well-formed SFP/DSL role?
o: A named backup, protected time and direct access to leaders
A volunteer deputy, flexible time and indirect access to leaders
A single holder, unlimited duties and full authority over discipline
A part-time post, fixed duties and no budget line allowed
why: A good role has a backup, protected time and direct access to leaders.

q: What does safe programming aim to do?
o: Making sure our work does not create or enable harm
Removing every risk so that no activity can ever fail
Replacing child protection programmes with general site safety measures only
Limiting all contact between staff and children at distant sites
why: Safe programming does not remove all risk. It ensures our work does not create or enable harm.

q: A school plans an overnight camp. What is the trigger for a safeguarding risk?
o: The overnight stay, which creates unsupervised contact at night
The harm a child could suffer during the night
The reputation damage that follows after a serious incident
The camp fee that families must pay before travel
why: A trigger is the situation that sets a risk in motion.

q: Staff share personal numbers and a group chat allows private contact with children. Which risk category fits?
o: Digital and information, because online channels allow private contact
Supply chain, because vendors supply the phones used there
Context and environment, because the community accepts online chatting
Partnerships, because partners always manage the group chat settings
why: Online platforms and personal numbers are digital and information risks.

q: Rushed recruitment, no reference checks and unsupervised volunteers belong to which category?
o: People, because unsuitable individuals gain access to children
Programme design, because safeguarding is missing from budget
Media, because a child's identity may be revealed
Supply chain, because vendors have no safeguarding clause
why: Weak recruitment lets unsuitable people reach children, which is a people risk.

q: At which stage do teams ask participants if they feel safe and check the register?
o: Monitoring, which also updates the risk assessment
Design, which also costs the mitigation properly
Start-up, which also vets staff and partners
Close-out, which also stores all records safely
why: Monitoring checks safety, the register and trends, and updates the risk assessment.

q: Which rule is correct for home visits to child domestic workers?
o: Visits are planned, logged, supervised and never made alone
Visits are spontaneous, informal, private and usually made alone
Visits are arranged through employers who stay in rooms
Visits are skipped whenever the employer objects to access
why: Home visits must be planned, logged and supervised, and never made alone.

q: A risk has Severe impact (4) and Likely likelihood (4). What are the score and the response?
o: 20, rated High, needing strong mitigation and sign-off
16, rated High, needing strong mitigation and sign-off
20, rated Extreme, needing immediate stop and escalation
24, rated Extreme, needing immediate stop and escalation
why: (4 x 4) + 4 = 20, which is High (15 to 21).

q: A risk has Extreme impact (5) but Rare likelihood (1). What is the result?
o: 10, rated Medium, needing mitigation, owners and monitoring
6, rated Low, needing only routine controls here
5, rated Low, treated like merely negligible impact
15, rated High, needing strong mitigation and sign-off
why: (5 x 1) + 5 = 10, which is Medium. Impact counts twice.

q: A risk has Significant impact (3) and Likely likelihood (4). What is the result?
o: 15, rated High, needing strong mitigation and sign-off
12, rated Medium, needing mitigation, owners and monitoring
9, rated Low, needing only routine controls here
18, rated High, needing immediate stop and escalation
why: (3 x 4) + 3 = 15, which is High.

q: A risk has Moderate impact (2) and Possible likelihood (3). What is the result?
o: 8, which is Low and managed with routine controls
6, which is Low and managed with routine controls
10, which is Medium and needs owners and monitoring
12, which is Medium and needs owners and monitoring
why: (2 x 3) + 2 = 8, which is Low (5 to 9).

q: Which formula gives the safeguarding risk score?
o: Impact multiplied by likelihood, then impact added again
Impact added to likelihood, then the total doubled
Likelihood multiplied by impact, then likelihood added again
Impact multiplied by likelihood, then divided by impact
why: Score = (Impact x Likelihood) + Impact.

q: Why does the formula add impact a second time?
o: Serious harm should still matter when it is unlikely
Unlikely events should always be ignored by planning teams
Frequent small harms should always outweigh rare severe harms
Donors prefer scores that reach higher numbers on charts
why: Impact counts twice so that serious harm still matters when it is unlikely.

q: Which score range means the activity must be stopped or redesigned and escalated now?
o: 22 or above, rated Extreme on the grid
15 to 21, rated High on the grid
10 to 14, rated Medium on the grid
5 to 9, rated Low on the grid
why: Extreme (22 and above) needs a stop or redesign and immediate escalation.

q: Which risk has the highest score?
o: Significant impact paired with near certain likelihood
Extreme impact paired with merely unlikely likelihood
Severe impact paired with merely possible likelihood
Moderate impact paired with near certain likelihood
why: (3 x 5) + 3 = 18, compared with 15, 16 and 12.

q: A High risk cannot be reduced with the resources available. What should happen next?
o: Escalate in writing, propose a decision and record who decided
Mention it in a hallway chat and wait for instructions
Lower the score until the activity fits the available resources
Proceed quietly and review the risk after the activity ends
why: Escalation should be in writing, with a proposed decision and a record of who decided.

q: Which is the correct order of the risk assessment procedure?
o: Identify risk, name who is at risk, score, act, assign owners, review
Score the risk, identify who is at risk, review, act, assign owners
Assign owners, identify risk, score, review, act, name who is at risk
Act, identify risk, assign owners, score, name who is at risk, review
why: The sequence is identify, who is at risk, score, act, owners and dates, review.

q: Which practice makes a venue safer for children?
o: Visitors sign in and are never left alone with children
Staff keep one locked room for private talks with children
Visitors may enter freely when they carry a donor badge
Children choose any hidden room for private games after class
why: Visitors must sign in and never be left alone with children.

q: What should every partner agreement include?
o: Safeguarding clauses and the code of conduct, signed and briefed
Payment terms and the delivery schedule, signed, dated and filed
Branding rules and the logo placement, signed, dated and approved
Insurance cover and the vehicle details, signed, dated and stored
why: Partners with access must sign safeguarding clauses and the code of conduct.

q: Why is an unmonitored risk plan weak?
o: Incomplete action is an incomplete process and leaves risk open
Plans change automatically when staff leave their current team roles
Donors always check each action before the whole activity starts
Written plans protect children even if nobody ever reads them
why: Plans that are not monitored leave the risks open.

q: Who should help identify risks?
o: Everyone, including participants and stakeholders, not just the safeguarding team
Only the safeguarding team, because it holds the formal training
Only the board, because it signs the final risk register
Only external auditors, because they remain fully independent of staff
why: Everyone helps identify risks, including participants.

q: Why use a conditional offer?
o: It becomes final only when every check is back and clear
It lets the new person start unsupervised work while checks continue
It reduces the salary until the first probation review finally ends
It prevents the person from reading the safeguarding policy too early
why: A conditional offer is final only when all checks are clear.

q: Which reference practice is correct?
o: Two references including the last employer, asked about conduct with children
One reference from a friend who confirms the candidate's good character
Two references from relatives who confirm the candidate's home address details
A verbal reference from a current senior colleague of the candidate
why: Use at least two references, including the last employer, and ask about conduct.

q: When should induction take place?
o: Within 30 days and before any unsupervised contact with children
Within one year and after the first yearly appraisal meeting
Within 30 days but only for staff who meet children
Within probation but only after the first donor visit ends
why: Induction is within 30 days and before unsupervised contact with children.

q: Which is a recruitment mistake?
o: Giving a good reference to push out someone with proven misconduct
Asking about employment gaps and why previous roles were ended early
Sharing the policy and code of conduct with candidates before interview
Keeping a checks tracker for every hire for easy later audit
why: References must be honest and include proven misconduct.

q: Reports rise after training and new channels are set up. What does this usually mean?
o: Trust is rising, not that harm is increasing
Harm is rising so training should be stopped
Staff are exaggerating so channels should be reduced
Registers are faulty so reports should be removed
why: Reports rising after training usually means trust is rising, not harm.

q: Which barrier is a trust-in-the-mechanism problem?
o: Fear of retaliation and doubt that reports are ever acted on
People not knowing the channel exists or how to find it
A false sense of community and silence seen as being normal
Power distance, respect for authority and a fear of local stigma
why: Fear of retaliation and doubt that reports are acted on are trust barriers.

q: Which first step best improves reporting in an organisation?
o: Assess whether people know, trust and can reach the channels
Buy a hotline number and print posters for all sites
Announce a zero tolerance rule and then wait for reports
Ask the employer to name which workers should report concerns
why: Assess first, then identify barriers, then act.

q: Who should log every report, and when?
o: A named person, in the register, on the same day
Any manager, in a personal notebook, within the next week
The reporter, in the public log, at the next meeting
The board, in the annual report, after the yearly audit
why: A named person should log every report in the register on the same day.

q: A child says: 'Please do not tell anyone.' Which reply is best?
o: Thank you for telling me; I must tell someone who can help
I promise to keep this secret forever between just you and me
Are you sure that is what happened? Please tell me every detail
I will go and speak to him first to hear his side
why: Never promise secrecy. Explain who you will tell and why.

q: Who should lead an investigation into an allegation against a staff member?
o: Trained independent investigators who have no link to the case
The SFP/DSL acting alone as the main interviewer on site
The line manager who supervises the person who is accused
Any friendly colleague who knows the child and the family
why: Investigators must be trained and independent, never the SFP/DSL alone.

q: In triage, what comes first?
o: Check for immediate danger and act on safety first
Record the full story in writing before anything else
Refer the person to legal services before danger checks
Inform the donor about the case before safety checks
why: Triage asks first whether anyone is in immediate danger.

q: A girl needs medical care after a sexual assault in Lagos. Where should she be referred?
o: A sexual assault referral centre, with her informed consent
A vocational training skills centre, with her informed consent
A local education authority office, with her informed consent
A state legal aid office, with her informed consent
why: Medical care after sexual assault is provided by sexual assault referral centres.

q: A group photo is taken from behind with no names and the location shown only as Lagos. What is still needed before posting?
o: Informed consent and a safeguarding sign-off before any release
A staff member's personal account to post it faster
A longer caption naming the area to help donors
Nothing more because the faces are not visible there
why: Consent and safeguarding sign-off are always needed.

q: What is the triangle of risk in media use?
o: Face, name and location, which must never appear together
Face, age and gender, which must never appear together
Name, school and class, which must never appear together
Location, date and time, which must never appear together
why: Face, name and location together lead someone straight to the child.

q: A participant says beating a child worker teaches discipline. What does the behaviour change method suggest?
o: Validate the concern, then correct and offer a replacement
Ignore the view and move to the next slide
Remove the participant and report the view to police
Agree with the view and then add a warning
why: Validate the thought, correct it, answer the fear and offer a replacement.

q: What keeps an action plan alive?
o: Named owners, dates, a monthly tracker and a named backup
Strong intentions, flexible dates, a yearly review and a champion
Shared ownership, open deadlines, a donor tracker and a deputy
Verbal promises, fixed dates, a board review and no backup
why: Owners, dates, monthly tracking and a backup keep the plan alive.
